Abstract
In prospective advancements, it is anticipated that software-defined networking (SDN) will establish itself as the principal 
framework for the implementation of heterogeneous networks. Unlike traditional networking paradigms, SDN differenti-
ates the control and data planes, thereby enabling enhanced routing and management of traffic across various domains. 
The controllers located within the control plane are responsible for programming the forwarding devices situated in 
the data plane, whereas the highest layer, referred to as the application plane, enforces regulatory policies and coordi-
nates network programming. Interfacing mechanisms are utilized across the different layers of SDN to ensure effective 
communication. Nonetheless, SDN faces challenges related to traffic distribution, such as load imbalance, which could 
negatively affect overall network performance. In response, developers have formulated a range of SDN load-balancing 
solutions intended to improve the efficiency of SDN. Furthermore, owing to the swift advancements in the domain 
of artificial intelligence (AI), researchers are investigating the viability of incorporating AI methodologies into SDN to 
optimize resource utilization and enhance overall performance. This survey is organized as follows: First, it provides an 
analysis of the SDN architecture and investigates the load balancing challenges present within SDN. Second, it classifies 
AI-driven load balancing strategies and critically assesses these mechanisms from multiple perspectives, including the 
algorithms/techniques utilized, the particular issues addressed, and their corresponding advantages and disadvantages. 
Third, it consolidates the metrics used to evaluate the effectiveness of these techniques. Finally, it identifies the emerging 
trends and challenges associated with AI-enhanced load balancing for future research endeavors.

As networks expand and the number of users and network traffic increases, traditional networks face challenges in 
network management due to proprietary network hardware devices like switches, routers, and load balancers [1].This

SDNs offer a centralized view of network resources by separating the control layer from the data layer, enabling 
advanced management [2]. Load balancing in SDNs involves distributing traffic across the network, a capability 
lacking in traditional networks To address the high volume of network traffic and congestion issues, load balancing 
strategies are implemented by controllers [3]. However, a single controller may not efficiently manage the entire

2.1  Software‑defined networks (SDN)
SDN has emerged as a revolutionary technology within the realm of computer networks and has garnered significant 
attention in recent times. The concept was first conceived during a collaborative endeavor in 2008 between Berkeley 
and Stanford universities [3]. SDN enables network researchers to streamline the management of network services by 
abstracting lower-level network functions in a more straightforward manner [4]. This methodology involves the segrega-
tion of network control, responsible for determining traffic routing, from data forwarding systems that guide traffic to its 
intended destination [3]. Consequently, this makes the network programmable directly by the network administrator, 
effectively separating the network infrastructure from network applications and services. Given that existing network 
architectures do not fully cater to the requirements of businesses and users, the gradual adoption of the SDN architecture 
as a standard in the development of network routers is addressing these crucial needs [1–3].
2.2  SDN architecture
The framework of Software-Defined Networking (SDN) exemplifies an innovative paradigm in network architecture. It 
enables a centralized controller to manage the entire network infrastructure comprehensively [2]. The OpenFlow protocol 
serves as the optimal mechanism for implementing SDN architecture [3]. When juxtaposed with traditional networks, 
the amalgamation of SDN architecture and the OpenFlow protocol provides network administrators with a superior 
strategy for flow management via controllers [3]. In conventional networking frameworks, the control and data planes 
are integrated within the physical hardware. In contrast, SDN architecture clearly delineates the network into a control 
plane and a data plane (forwarding plane) [3, 4]. The control plane, typically comprising one or multiple controllers, func-
tions as the intelligent element of the network, regulating the entire system. Conversely, the data plane is constituted 
by the actual network hardware, such as routers, switches, and middle boxes, which facilitate data transmission [4]. The 
SDN architecture is categorized into three fundamental planes as delineated by the Open Networking Foundation (ONF). 
The architectural framework is depicted in Fig. 1.
•	 Data Plane: This layer represents the essential foundation of the Software-Defined Networking (SDN) framework, 
encapsulating the physical network infrastructure. It includes forwarding devices such as routers, physical and virtual 
switches, and access points, primarily responsible for data packet forwarding based on defined protocols established 
on the flow tables by the SDN controller [4].
•	 Control Plane: This layer acts as the intermediary within the SDN architecture, enabling control functionalities through 
software-based SDN controllers that regulate the forwarding behavior of network switches. The controller manages 
these switches to relay packets according to specific instructions and provides a centralized view of the infrastruc-
ture for higher layers, employing a southbound API and OpenFlow protocol for device interaction, alongside a load 
balancer for implementing load balancing algorithms [4].
•	 Application Plane: This layer consists of various end-user applications that leverage the centralized perspective of 
the underlying infrastructure to inform their decision-making processes. Developers utilize the northbound API to 
connect with the SDN controller during application implementation, serving as a software intermediary between 
SDN applications and the controller platform components [4].

2.3  The significance of load balancing in software‑defined networking (SDN).
The processing capabilities of networks must increase in correlation with rising access and data traffic. Upgrading existing 
hardware to meet these demands incurs high costs and leads to resource inefficiency [3]. Load balancing (LB) distributes 
simultaneous traffic across multiple computing devices, enhancing processing capacity and reducing user response 
times, predominantly in enterprise application servers and web servers. While the financial implications of load balancers 
can be substantial, their operation is dictated by specific software, necessitating specialized administrators to optimize 
performance [2, 3]. Software-Defined Networking (SDN) enhances load balancing by providing a centralized perspective 
of resources, enabling improved management, flexibility, and overall network efficiency.
3  Classification of software centric network load balancing
The classification of network software-defined networks load balancing is examined in this section. In a specific paper [3], 
network software-defined networks load balancing is categorized into data page load balancing and control page load 
balancing. Illustrated in Fig. 2, the green segments in the tree diagram correspond to the sections in paper [3]. Neverthe-
less, certain papers address data page load balancing and control page load balancing simultaneously. Consequently, 
this paper classifies network software-defined networks load balancing into three distinct categories: data page load 
balancing, control page load balancing, and simultaneous data and control page load balancing. The green segments 
in the tree diagram have been included in this paper, offering a more intricate framework for network software-defined 
networks load balancing.

A.	 Static server load balancing
Static load balancing algorithms are appropriate for networks with indistinguishable servers but are unsuitable for 
dynamic networks due to their lack of adaptability [8].
B.	 Dynamic server load balancing
Dynamic server load balancing algorithms initially assess the present condition of servers and subsequently select 
an appropriate server-centric network load balancing scheme for traffic reception based on the obtained status [3].
Abdelltif et al. [9] proposed a cloud server load balancing service (SBLB) leveraging Software Defined Networking 
(SDN) to optimize resource usage and reduce user Latency. The methodology incorporates an application module on 
an SDN controller for server pool aggregation, utilizing OpenFlow switches for connectivity, while the controller man-
ages communications and host availability in real-time, with experimental results confirming the system’s effectiveness.
Zhong et al. [10] introduced a dynamic load balancing strategy, LBBSRT, predicated on server response time within 
the software-defined networks architecture. Their system model comprises three components: server, client switch Open 
Flow, and software-defined network controller. To distribute the load among servers, it evaluates the response time of 
all servers and allocates the load based on response time, prioritizing servers with lower or more stable response times. 
The method computes the minimum and maximum response times of servers and the disparity between them. A small 
disparity indicates similar server loads, favoring a server with the minimum response time. Otherwise, it computes the 
standard deviation, giving precedence to a server with a lower standard deviation for incoming load, i.e., a server with a 
more consistent response time. This approach surpasses the Random Round Robin technique, proving more cost-effective 
than conventional methods owing to reduced hardware and software customization requirements, although it may not 
effectively address server power conservation in numerous load balancing scenarios.
A Load Balancing (LB) algorithm delineated in [11] models the network as a graph, utilizing edges to signify channels 
and vertices for switches, thereby prioritizing bandwidth to optimize path selection and enhance Quality of Service (QoS) 
metrics. This two-phase methodology identifies the least loaded server and the most efficient route to it, although it 
notably lacks crucial QoS parameters, such as cost optimization, which are vital for assessing network Latency.
3.1.2  Link load balancing
Traffic is directed through the links to the servers, but these links could also face additional load. Consequently, the 
selection of the least congested link is made for routing the traffic [3].
Chen et al. [12] propose a framework, Traffic Prediction-based Energy Efficiency Optimization (TPEO), aimed at improv-
ing energy efficiency in software-defined networks through traffic prediction while addressing the balance between 
network load and energy consumption. An adaptive traffic monitoring mechanism is implemented to dynamically adjust 
monitoring periods for accurate real-time traffic load capture, thereby reducing monitoring costs. Furthermore, a novel 
online exploratory algorithm is introduced to optimize energy efficiency based on predictive models, facilitating load 
balancing, though it may inadvertently concentrate network traffic, increasing the risk of link failures.
Duong et al. [13] have introduced a novel load-balanced routing algorithm under quality of service constraints for wire-
less mesh networks. The algorithm, named Load-Balanced Routing under Quality of Transmission Constraints (LBRCQT), 
operates on the principle of centralized routing within a software-defined network controller. This algorithm is designed 
to enhance network performance in terms of signal-to-noise ratio (SNR), packet delivery ratio (PDR), and power.
Han et al. [14] have proposed a methodology for deploying a service function chain based on network debt theory. 
Initially, a set of potential key nodes is identified to establish a directed network. Subsequently, the deployment 
issue is converted into a problem of determining the optimal path within the directed network. In the final stage, 
a minimum cost maximum flow algorithm is utilized to identify the optimal deployment path and accomplish the 
deployment of the service function chain, taking into account link transmission cost as a cost factor and bandwidth 
demand as a constraint.

Andjamba et al. [15] present a load balancing routing protocol (LBRP) within software-defined networks to ensure 
optimal video quality during playback in manipulated software. This protocol utilizes a traffic engineering approach 
to achieve quality of service by categorizing traffic flows into two groups: 1- Latency-sensitive flows (real flows) and 
2- Non-latency-sensitive flows (non-real flows). Real flows are given higher priority and are directed through links with 
guaranteed bandwidth, while non-real flows are routed through different links. This enhancement enhances the user 
experience for various applications.
Galán et al. [16] tackle the challenge of traffic load balancing and minimizing energy consumption in an IP/SDN 
network. The migration from traditional IP networks to software-defined networks necessitates the replacement of IP 
network equipment with SDN-compatible devices. However, transitioning large networks is complex and must be con-
ducted gradually, leading to the establishment of a unified IP/SDN network. This study leverages the software-defined 
network model to distribute traffic among SDN switches and balance link loads. Furthermore, genetic algorithms are 
employed to optimize power usage by determining the most efficient network configuration with minimal active links, 
considering link capacities and existing traffic. This methodology results in a 50% decrease in maximum link utilization 
and a 60% reduction in energy consumption.
3.1.3  Simultaneous server and link load balancing
In the process of load balancing, the link traffic and server are evenly distributed at the same time through the application 
of the link load balancing algorithm towards the designated server. Simultaneously, the server load balancing algorithm 
is employed to ensure balanced distribution of workload between the server and link.
The study described in reference [17] focuses on load balancing in network software and employs machine learning 
methods like Artificial Neural Networks (ANN) and Reinforcement Learning to balance server load and route network 
software environments simultaneously. Server load balancing is achieved through an ANN that learns to distribute traffic 
among servers based on past learning experiences. Initially, the load balancer uses algorithms such as Least Connection 
Weighted Round Robin and Random Round Robin to gather server parameters including processor usage, memory usage, 
file type requested, bytes sent to the client, and bytes received. Subsequently, it learns patterns and constructs a model 
based on these parameters and algorithms. For path-based load balancing, the study utilizes the Abilene topology to 
evenly distribute the load across paths by identifying the most suitable paths from the client to the server.
Zheng et al. [18] have introduced the Network Load Balancing Algorithm for Software-defined networks based on 
Improved Ant Colony Optimization (IACO-LB). This research initially gathers comprehensive information about servers 
and links, which is then fed as input to the Ant Colony Optimization algorithm. The algorithm selects the least congested 
server and path. While this method exhibits stable and significant convergence speed, it neglects the consideration of 
controller processing costs.
A novel framework utilizing software-defined networking has been introduced to address the quality of service 
demands for diverse Internet of Things (IoT) applications while simultaneously achieving traffic equilibrium among IoT 
servers. The authors establish that the dual challenges are NP-hard and subsequently decompose the issue into server 
selection and path selection to mitigate time complexity. This tri-layered framework operates through interrelated inter-
faces, employing the Normalised Least Connection Mean Squares (NLMS) algorithm and a fuzzy system to optimize 
server capacity and load distribution according to traffic class quality [19]. In the following Table 2 there is an overview 
of data page load balancing papers.

In the vertical hierarchical controller system, individual controllers are situated at distinct levels, prohibiting commu-
nication between controllers on the same level, with all controllers overseen by a central controller [20]. Ejazet al. [21] 
have demonstrated the achievement of traffic load distribution through the utilization of a software-defined network 
(SDN) virtual network controller functioning as a virtual network function. The virtualization of network functions offers a 
viable solution for virtual network functions and associated services within a constantly changing network environment. 
Through the employment of a software-defined virtual network controller as a virtual network function, the capability to 
incorporate additional similar virtual network functions is facilitated, allowing for the expansion of secondary software-
defined virtual networks as traffic demands escalate. As the entirety of resources transitions to a virtual realm, the alloca-
tion of hardware resources can be dynamically adjusted in response to demand fluctuations. Upon the identification of a 
necessity for a secondary software-defined virtual network controller, a duplicate of the primary software-defined virtual 
network controller is generated with a congruent configuration to ensure accurate operation and equitable distribution 
of traffic. These two software-defined virtual network controllers are independently positioned in the cloud space, guar-
anteeing transparency and awareness among network clients regarding the creation of the supplementary software-
defined virtual network controller. Experimental findings substantiate the superiority of the proposed approach over 
existing methodologies, showcasing enhancements in load balancing of up to 14 percent under specific circumstances.
B.	  Distributed hierarchical model predictive controller
In the hierarchical controller, each controller is positioned within a layer in the horizontal controller. Consequently, 
despite operating in distinct domains, all controllers are regarded as primary controllers well-versed in the overall net-
work status [22].
Mokhtar et al. [23] proposed a Multi-Threshold Load Balancing (MTLB) migration scheme aimed at achieving continu-
ous load balancing among controllers. This scheme accurately identifies load status and adjusts thresholds dynamically 
as load levels change. It categorizes load into gradual levels to facilitate switch migration and implements a synchro-
nous load information synchronization strategy based on multi-threshold concept. By notifying other controllers when 
a threshold is reached or approached, it minimizes the overhead from inadvertent load information synchronization. 
The study also presents a methodology for migration operations by analyzing the behavior of migrating switches and 
controllers. Testing different reductions in migration numbers led to the selection of a response time threshold based 
on unique characteristics. By comparing response times of all controllers to this threshold, servers are categorized into 
heavy load and light load, and switches are migrated accordingly. This proactive scheme efficiently addresses uneven 
load distribution and reduces the time needed to resolve overloaded controllers.
Xiang et al. [24] proposed a deep reinforcement learning (DRL) framework aimed at resolving the switch migration 
problem (SMP) in software-defined networks, utilizing a two-dimensional matrix to represent network states as input 
for migration decision-making. To mitigate issues of overestimation and oscillation, a Double Deep Q-Network (DDQN) 
is employed and trained via experience replay, demonstrating notable improvements in load balancing and expediting 
the convergence to a balanced state.
Sahoo et al. [25] have introduced a load balancing framework known as Efficient Switch Migration Load Balancing 
(ESMLE), which is designed to efficiently assign switches to underutilized controllers. The framework employs a priority-
based ordering technique for controller selection, resembling an ideal solution. It enables flexible decision-making pro-
cesses for choosing controllers with varying resource characteristics. The TOPSIS method is utilized for decision analysis 
to rank controllers based on specific criteria such as current memory usage, CPU load, controller bandwidth status, and 
number of hops utilized. The advantages of this switch migration approach include effective load balancing, improved 
congestion reduction, and reduced migration time. However, a limitation of this method is the lack of consideration for 
traffic demand, making it more suitable for smaller environments.
Zhong et al. [26] introduced an advanced migration framework for load balancer software utilizing predictive load 
forecasting across multiple distributed controllers. This framework employs historical traffic data to anticipate future 
loads, thereby optimizing switch migration processes while minimizing communication overhead and migration fre-
quency through a dual-weight migration strategy.

3.3  Simultaneous balancing of the data and control sides
In contemporary network infrastructures, there is a significant challenge posed by the high volumes of traffic, leading to 
congestion on the data side. The issue arises when attempting to balance the load on the data side with a single control-
ler, which can become a bottleneck. As networks expand continuously, a solitary controller is insufficient to effectively 
manage the entire network, diminishing scalability and availability. Consequently, a distributed controller architecture 
is employed, allowing for the utilization of multiple controllers on the control side and enabling load balancing among 
them. While switch migration facilitates load balancing in the control plane, it can create an imbalance in the servers. 
To address this concern, researchers have endeavored to achieve simultaneous load balancing on both the data and 
control sides. This type of load balancing can be categorized into two main types: server and controller load balancing, 
and link and controller load balancing.
3.3.1  Equal load balancer and controller
A.	  Dynamic load balancing and logical concentration/distribution controller
Guo et al. [28] introduced a strategy known as Load Variance Synchronization (LVS) to enhance load balancing in a multi-
domain SDN network with multiple controllers. The method aims to address issues such as loop formation caused by 
conflicting server data and synchronization overhead. This is achieved through two specific schemes: Minimum Load 
Server State Synchronization (LSVS) and Minimum Load Domain Variance Synchronization (LDVS). LVS has demonstrated 
improved load balancing performance and reduced synchronization overhead compared to existing techniques. How-
ever, the effectiveness of the proposed methods has not yet been tested in a real-world setting, and factors such as 
energy consumption and latency have not been thoroughly examined.
B.	  Dynamic server load balancing and distributed controllers
3.4  Hierarchical vertical dynamic server load balancing and distributed controllers
Liet al. [29] have presented a technique for positioning a dependable controller through the optimization of latency and 
load. Their multi-objective optimization approach takes into account the latency among controllers, controller latency to 
the switch, and load distribution. Initially, the optimization goal is defined, and a model of controller layout is formulated 
utilizing the LOCP algorithm for optimizing latency and load distribution. For the logical allotment of computational 
resources, the HACA algorithm is applied, which is a resource allocation technique grounded on latency restrictions 
and dependability, also taking into account a multi-objective constraint-based latency and reliability technique. The 
constraint objective is initially introduced, and a model of resource allocation established for the constraint objective 
based on latency restrictions and dependability. Empirical findings indicate that the LOCP algorithm enhances controller 
load distribution by 18.36% in comparison to other algorithms, while ensuring reduced propagation latency and queue 
latency. The HACA algorithm effectively addresses the resource allocation issue for workers, decreasing worker response 
time and average completion latency. Limitations of this approach include 1- a low comprehensive number of optimiza-
tion criteria when considering the controller placement optimization criteria, and 2- a higher consideration of network 
component failures over single link failures when addressing the issue of placing a reliable controller.

a) 	 Reinforcement learning
This paper discusses a machine learning approach that involves learning through interactions with the environ-
ment to accomplish a specific objective [33]. In their study [17], the authors employed a reinforcement learning 
technique to distribute the workload across links. Initially, the links are placed in a learning table, and the optimal

latency is prioritized for selection.
Filali et al. [34] introduced a reinforcement learning algorithm to address the challenge of balancing barbin con-
trollers and the migration cost based on controller response time. The algorithm incorporates two winning actions 
and one losing action. The winning actions result in a reward, with the first one aiming to minimize load balance 
and the second one focusing on load balance optimization while avoiding switch migration. The losing action, on 
the other hand, involves switch migration. The priority is given to the first winning action over the second, while 
the losing action leads to high load balance and numerous migrations, indicating a lack of control balance in the 
software-defined network but with substantial migration costs. Decisions are made based on these actions, with 
rewards or penalties assigned accordingly, allowing for experiential learning.
Yeo et al. [35] investigated the implementation of distributed controllers in software-defined networking (SDN), 
emphasizing their enhanced scalability and reliability over traditional static mappings which lead to imbalanced load 
distributions. They proposed a reinforcement learning-based strategy, Switch Load-aware Reinforcement Learning 
(SAR-LE), which optimally allocates resources by assessing the utilization ratios of switches and controllers, while 
treating switches as agents within the learning framework. Experimental results revealed that SAR-LE significantly 
improves load distribution efficiency among SDN controllers, achieving a reduction in normalized standard devia-
tion by as much as 34%.
In 2018, Li et al. [36] presented a study titled "SDN Controller Load Balancing Based on Reinforcement Learning." The 
study proposes a load balancing controller mechanism that utilizes reinforcement learning to facilitate local load balanc-
ing within specified networks through software deployment. By measuring the load ratio deviation between controllers, 
the study determines the initial exit migration domain and migration within the domain. A three-stage initial migration 
process, involving the mentioned migration domain and a group of switches acting as a migration domain, is shown 
to enhance local migration efficiency. By employing reinforcement learning to select multiple sets of triples for final 
migration, the study demonstrates that global optimal load balancing with minimal cost can be achieved without migra-
tion conflicts and ensuring the best overall migration performance. Empirical evidence suggests that this mechanism 
optimally utilizes controller resources, effectively balancing load between controllers, reducing unnecessary migration 
overhead, and improving response time to incoming packet requests.
In a distinct investigation, Zhang et al. [37] introduced a novel critical flow rerouting reinforcement learning strategy 
(CFR-RL), which employs reinforcement learning to autonomously establish a critical flow selection approach independ-

unseen traffic matrices. In parallel,

Metaheuristic algorithms are deemed appropriate for addressing intricate optimization challenges that cannot be fea-

A) Genetic Algorithm (GA) is a computational method that leverages principles from natural genetics and evolutionary 
theory to explore solution spaces [5, 42]. Sun et al. implemented the Genetic Algorithm in [44] to optimize controller 
placement for reducing switch latency. Another study [14] utilized the Genetic Algorithm for energy conservation, where 
network configuration is encoded into a chromosome with constraints such as link capacities and traffic volume. The 
objective is to minimize active links for enhanced energy efficiency.
B) Ant Colony Optimization (ACO) emulates ant behavior to tackle problem-solving tasks [43]. In [18], it was applied for 
server and link load balancing, with the algorithm selecting the least loaded server and guiding ants along the shortest 
path with more pheromones to find the optimal route. In a different context [29], the resource allocation problem was 
approached as a multi-objective optimization issue, being addressed through an exploratory ant colony algorithm. The 
system has m servers and n types of computation requests, and the warmth distribution of each computation type is 
determined through an ant colony algorithm with m.
C) Particle Swarm Optimization (PSO) algorithm replicates the flocking behavior of birds [44]. In [45], the PSO algorithm 
was applied to handle the controller placement problem considering controller latency and capacity constraints. The 
algorithm performs parallel searches on multiple particles to find the optimal solution iteratively, which results in the 
placement of the controller with minimum latency.
D) Using genetic algorithms and particle swarming algorithms In [29], the PSO algorithm was utilized to cluster domain 
controllers in software-defined networks due to the adverse effects of improper segmentation on controller loads. By 
integrating Genetic Algorithm and PSO algorithm in [24], a solution was proposed for distributed controller placement 
to mitigate latencys and imbalances in controller loads within software-defined networks. Although a multi-objective

mance through the reduction of migration and the utilization of genetic and particle swarm algorithms. The procedure 
commences with the identification of the controller by employing a balanced or unbalanced threshold, followed by the 
application of particles swarm algorithm and genetic algorithms for switching. The method entails the selection of target 
controllers for migration switches and their respective costs via genetic algorithms, which are subsequently inputted 
into the particle swarm algorithm to determine the optimal solution for relocating the switch to the suitable controller.

5  Prediction in software based network load balancing
Prediction methods are employed in software-based network load balancing to forecast controller load, server load, 
and traffic, leading to load balancing and decreased energy consumption. Among various forecasting approaches, time 
series forecasting methods are predominantly utilized in this context due to their periodic sampling of time series predic-
tions at fixed intervals for resource management and load balancing purposes. Consequently, a time series is generated 
consisting of a sequence of recent observations, which is then used by time series methods to predict future values. 
Notable time series forecasting methods include Autoregressive Integrated Moving Average (ARIMA), Normalized Least 
Mean Squares (NLMS), and Long Short Term Memory (LSTM).
Normalised Least Mean Squares: Minimum prediction: The future workload prediction is based on the normalized 
least mean square method [50]. paper [51] also utilizes normalized least mean square to forecast server loads, leading 
to load balancing and decreased energy consumption. By accurately predicting server loads, underutilized servers can 
be shut down to lower energy usage, while additional servers can be added during peak times to prevent overload. 
The Auto regression Integrated Moving Average model assumes future variable values to be a linear combination 
of past workload and random errors, preventing controller overload. For instance, a switch migration scheduling 
algorithm can transfer switches from overloaded to under loaded controllers.
Autoregression integrated moving average: In the auto regression integrated moving average model, it is postulated 
that forthcoming values of a specific variable can be expressed as a linear amalgamation of preceding workload and 
stochastic deviations [52]. The study highlighted in reference [34] employs the autoregression integrated moving 
average technique to anticipate the magnitude of switch load and avert controller overload. Consequently, a switch 
migration scheduling algorithm is implemented to transfer certain switches from the overwhelmed controller to the 
less burdened controller.
Short-term long-term memory: A neural network form is recursive and has a powerful ability to remember for the 
purpose of prediction [53]. in the study [12], short-term long-term memory is utilized within a recurrent network 
to forecast traffic patterns, aiming to evenly distribute the load on network links and optimize energy utilization. 
This predictive approach enables the deactivation of devices with excess load to reduce energy consumption, while 
ensuring devices can be activated to balance the load during potential future congestion scenarios.

challenges derived from the literature reviewed.

overhead costs. Distributing controllers across multiple domains presents a viable solution; however, this increases 
deployment expenses and diminishes operational efficiency. Current strategies have not adequately addressed the

2.	 Initially, Software-Defined Networking (SDN) was primarily utilized within small enterprise frameworks, but recent

4.	 Most existing load-balancing methods neglect the critical issues of energy conservation and carbon emissions, 
which could significantly enhance their effectiveness and appeal. Consequently, future research should prioritize 
load-balancing frameworks that integrate considerations of energy utilization and carbon footprint.

8  Conclusion
Various approaches exist for distributing workloads efficiently in software-defined networks. This paper delves into a 
more comprehensive categorization of load balancing techniques within software-defined networks. Broadly speaking, 
these techniques can be classified into three main groups: data plane load balancing, control plane load balancing, and 
the combined management of data and control plane load balancing. Each of these categories is examined, followed by 
a discussion on optimization strategies leveraging artificial intelligence. In recent times, predictive methodologies have 
gained prominence in facilitating load distribution in software-defined networks, showcasing their versatility across 
various load balancing aspects within such networks. Notably, the incorporation of predictive techniques in network 
load balancing has not only enhanced efficiency but also contributed towards energy conservation in software-defined 
networks, underscoring the pivotal role of load prediction in curbing energy consumption.

Abstract: In prospective advancements, it is anticipated that software-defined networking (SDN) will establish itself as the principal framework for the implementation of heterogeneous networks. Unlike traditional networking paradigms, SDN differenti- ates the control and data planes, thereby enabling enhanced routing and management of traffic across various domains. The controllers located within the control plane are responsible for programming the forwarding devices situated in the data plane, whereas the highest layer, referred to as the application plane, enforces regulatory policies and coordi- nates network programming. Interfacing mechanisms are utilized across the different layers of SDN to ensure effective communication. Nonetheless, SDN faces challenges related to traffic distribution, such as load imbalance, which could negatively affect overall network performance. In response, developers have formulated a range of SDN load-balancing solutions intended to improve the efficiency of SDN. Furthermore, owing to the swift advancements in the domain of artificial intelligence (AI), researchers are investigating the viability of incorporating AI methodologies into SDN to optimize resource utilization and enhance overall performance. This survey is organized as follows: First, it provides an analysis of the SDN architecture and investigates the load balancing challenges present within SDN. Second, it classifies AI-driven load balancing strategies and critically assesses these mechanisms from multiple perspectives, including the algorithms/techniques utilized, the particular issues addressed, and their corresponding advantages and disadvantages. Third, it consolidates the metrics used to evaluate the effectiveness of these techniques. Finally, it identifies the emerging trends and challenges associated with AI-enhanced load balancing for future research endeavors.
